title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pair_count = 200), consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). A randomized 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements; however, the explicit selection seed for that holdout is not present among labeled artifacts, a reproducibility gap we document. Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank under the frozen shared‑initial policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, exact inferential output, and an artifact‑grounded interpretation of operational implications and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models offers operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. Whether automated repair materially reduces unsafe changes depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator and sampling policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity to the operational semantics of interest, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study uses a paired design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, issuing one automated repair on that identical candidate.
sections.related_work: Empirical surveys and studies document that large language models produce factual errors, hallucinations, and prompt‑sensitive non‑determinism; mitigation proposals include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained generation, and guarded agent architectures. Prototype work in NetOps shows feasibility of intent→configuration generation but typically lacks instrumented, preregistered, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectures combining LLM generation with deterministic validators or emulators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers, Mininet emulation) are common proposals; red‑team audits and agent‑audit studies highlight configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our confirmatory run addresses a specific operational question—marginal benefit of deterministic GVR under a fixed shared‑initial generation policy—and situates itself as an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that complements earlier prototype and threat studies.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration. The experiment was preregistered (study id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) as a paired binary comparison with n = 200 tasks. For each task a single deterministic initial LLM output was produced and reused for both conditions: (A) baseline — apply the generator output unchecked to the primary deterministic validator; (B) guarded (GVR) — validate the same generator output and, if the validator reported violations, issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM and re‑validate the repaired candidate. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729.

Task bank and validators. The curated, machine‑checkable task bank comprised 200 intent→configuration tasks distributed across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encoded initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima) and a required_sequence that the deterministic validator enforces. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) evaluates syntactic correctness, intent constraints, and structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent secondary disagreement detector and was executed on a randomized 10% holdout to detect validator blind spots. We document that the artifact reporting the holdout’s contamination summary records zero disagreements; we also document that the explicit selection seed for that holdout is missing from labeled artifacts and therefore exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout draw is not possible.

Adapter semantics and determinism. The adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate that both conditions evaluated. The preserved execution traces show hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations across the sample. The declared model configuration records the model label (gpt‑5‑mini) and a null temperature field ("temperature": null) in the archived configuration. Because the model configuration does not record an explicit numeric temperature, determinism for this run was achieved by adapter‑enforced shared‑initial semantics and audited single invocations rather than by an explicit recorded model parameter value; the adapter’s audited accounting is the evidence that a single deterministic generation was used per task.

Repair budget, stopping, and handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; maximum allowed model calls were 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs). The adapter enforced the cap. Missingness rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure failures; tasks flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would be excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan, with sensitivity analyses preregistered for alternative treatments. All decisions and audit fields (episode accounting, model‑call counts, and validator diagnostics) are archived in the execution bundle.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. Run execution completed all planned episodes and pairs: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter accounting audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming the preregistered single shared initial invocation semantics. There were no technical failures affecting the primary analysis: missingness_summary records complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes.

Primary outcomes and inferential results. The primary deterministic validator reported success on every initial candidate: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline validator failure prevalence was zero on this sample under the frozen shared‑initial policy, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis requiring a ≥50% relative reduction could not be evaluated.

Secondary checks and repairs. Because no initial validator failures occurred, the repair branch was never invoked; consequently, secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are empty for this run. The preregistered Mininet holdout (20 tasks) returned zero validator–emulator disagreements in the contamination summary; we note again that the labeled artifact set does not include the explicit randomized selection seed used for the holdout, limiting the ability to deterministically reconstruct the exact holdout draw despite the zero‑disagreement finding.

Representative diagnostics. Representative per‑task validator traces show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0 for tasks labeled with difficulty levels such as "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" and patterns (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). These traces document that tasks exercised nontrivial dependency constraints while the generator produced validator‑satisfying sequences under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed null result (no validator‑detected failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical outcome: under the constrained shared‑initial paired design and the chosen generator/prompt policy, there were no validator‑detectable errors for GVR to reduce. The exact inferential outputs (p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]) precisely encode that fact for this sample and design. This does not imply that GVR cannot be beneficial in other settings; rather, it clarifies that the marginal utility of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage for the workload and generation policy used.

Methodological tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator+repair on the identical generator output, enhancing internal causal control but excluding benefits obtainable by re‑sampling the model or using stochastic sampling strategies. An unconditional operational risk assessment (probability that an LLM pipeline produces an unsafe candidate on an arbitrary invocation) would instead require independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws or higher‑temperature sampling to estimate baseline failure prevalence and repair efficacy under realistic stochasticity.

Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators are necessary but not sufficient oracles for operational safety. The Mininet emulator was included to detect validator blind spots at the data‑plane level; the holdout produced zero disagreements in this run, but the missing labeled selection seed for the holdout imposes a reproducibility limitation. Robust operational assurance requires diverse validators, larger emulation sampling, vendor‑specific semantics, and adversarial perturbation tests to probe validator blind spots more comprehensively.

Practical implications. For practitioners, the run suggests two complementary predeployment measurements: (1) empirically measure baseline validator failure prevalence for the intended generator/sampling policy on representative workloads; (2) expand validator fidelity via emulation or selective device checks. If baseline failures are rare under the production policy, a single‑pass automated repair budget yields limited marginal safety returns for validator‑detected errors and resources may be better allocated to validator expansion and adversarial testing. Conversely, when baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with an adequate repair budget can reduce validator‑detected errors, a hypothesis that the present artifact bundle documents structurally but does not empirically demonstrate because no repairs were invoked here.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), resulting in an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value is workload and policy dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, automated repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived under the preregistration id cited in the Disclosure Statement for independent inspection.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
